details:
**The Beatitudes**
The series of blessings that opens the sermon, such as "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven," "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth," and blessings for those who mourn and for the peacemakers. Matthew has eight or nine of them, depending on how they are counted; Luke's shorter parallel, the Sermon on the Plain, has four, paired with four woes.

**The Lord's Prayer ("Our Father")**
The model prayer Jesus teaches in Matthew 6, beginning "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name" and including "Give us today our daily bread." Its Greek word for "daily," epiousios, appears nowhere else, and Jerome's Vulgate rendered it "supersubstantial" in Matthew. The closing doxology "for thine is the kingdom, the power, and the glory" is found in later Byzantine-type manuscripts and is generally considered a later addition.

**"Salt of the earth" and "light of the world"**
Jesus calls his listeners the salt of the earth, asking what can restore salt that has lost its savor, and the light of the world, like a city on a hill. He adds that no one lights a candle (lamp) and puts it under a bushel; it goes on a candlestick to give light to the whole house.

**Wise and foolish builders**
The parable that closes the sermon. Whoever hears and does Jesus's words is like a wise man who built his house on the rock, which stood through rain and floods; whoever ignores them is like a foolish man who built his house on the sand, which fell.

**"Consider the lilies of the field"**
Jesus tells his audience not to worry about food or clothing. The fowls (birds) of the air are fed without sowing or reaping and the lilies grow without toiling or spinning, and he asks whether worrying can add a cubit to one's height or an hour to one's life; "take no thought for the morrow."

**"Turn the other cheek"**
Jesus replaces "an eye for an eye" with "resist not evil": if someone strikes your right cheek, offer the other. He also says to give your cloak to someone who takes your coat, and if forced to go one mile, go two (the origin of "go the extra mile"), and to love your enemies.

**The Antitheses ("You have heard it said... but I say unto you")**
A section of Matthew 5 in which Jesus quotes a commandment of the Mosaic Law and then makes it stricter. Anger and calling a brother "Raca" (a term of contempt) put one in danger of the council, looking at a woman with lust is already adultery in the heart, and instead of swearing oaths (even by your own head, since you cannot make one hair white or black) you should "let your yes be yes." The chapter ends with "Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect."

**Matthew chapters 5–7**
The sermon is the first of Jesus's five major discourses in the Gospel of Matthew, given early in his ministry. He goes up a mountain in Galilee to deliver it, traditionally placed at the Mount of Beatitudes near the Sea of Galilee.

**The Cost of Discipleship by Dietrich Bonhoeffer**
A 1937 book by the German Lutheran pastor and anti-Nazi dissident, a large part of which is a commentary on the Sermon on the Mount. It contrasts "cheap grace," meaning forgiveness without repentance or obedience, with "costly grace," which demands that one follow Christ.

**False prophets: "figs from thistles"**
Jesus warns of false prophets who come in sheep's clothing but are inwardly ravenous wolves. He asks whether people gather grapes from thorns or figs from thistles, and says "by their fruits ye shall know them."

**"Judge not" and the speck and the beam**
Jesus says "Judge not, that ye be not judged," and asks why one sees the speck (mote) in a brother's eye while ignoring the beam (plank) in one's own. He tells hypocrites to first remove the beam from their own eye.

**"Pearls before swine"**
The sermon is the source of the saying not to give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine, lest they trample them and turn on you. It warns against offering precious teachings to those who will only scorn them.

**"No man can serve two masters"**
Jesus says no one can serve both God and mammon (wealth), and urges storing up treasure in heaven rather than on earth, "for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." The same chapter says the eye is the lamp of the body and that almsgiving, prayer, and fasting should be done in secret, not to be seen by others.

**"Ask, and it shall be given you," the Golden Rule, and the narrow gate**
In Matthew 7 Jesus promises "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you." The chapter also gives the Golden Rule (do to others what you would have them do to you) and contrasts the wide gate that leads to destruction with the narrow gate that leads to life.

**New Moses and Luther's interpretation**
Many interpreters see Jesus teaching the law from a mountain as a parallel to Moses receiving the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai, with Jesus as a "new Moses." Martin Luther rejected the Catholic reading that its hardest commands were "counsels of perfection" for monks and clergy, and argued that they govern the Christian's personal, spiritual life rather than the work of governments.
